items.followUp: Describe how atomic size changes down a group and across a period.

rubric.why: Tests the trend across a period.
rubric.description: Electronegativity increases from left to right across a period.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the correct direction across a period.

rubric.why: Tests the trend down a group.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the correct direction down a group.

modelAnswer: Electronegativity generally increases from left to right across a period.
It generally decreases from top to bottom down a group.

items.followUp: Explain why atomic size increases down a group.

rubric.why: The increased nuclear charge is the cause of stronger attraction across a period.
rubric.description: Nuclear charge increases from left to right because the number of protons increases.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking the across-period increase to nuclear charge or proton number.

rubric.why: The stronger attraction draws the electron cloud closer to the nucleus.
rubric.description: Added electrons enter the same shell, so the stronger nuclear attraction pulls them closer and decreases atomic size.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that electrons enter the same shell and are pulled closer.

modelAnswer: From left to right, the nuclear charge increases as the number of protons increases.
The added electrons enter the same shell, so the stronger attraction pulls them closer to the nucleus and atomic size decreases.

items.followUp: How many elements are present in each of the second and third periods?

rubric.why: Assesses the number of periods described as normal.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving the number two.

rubric.why: Identifies which periods are meant and their characteristic length.
rubric.description: The second and third periods are the normal periods, each containing eight elements.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the second and third periods, or stating that each has eight elements.

modelAnswer: There are two normal periods: the second and the third periods.
Each of these periods contains eight elements.

items.followUp: Differentiate between a shared pair and a non-bonding pair of electrons.

rubric.why: A bond pair is defined by sharing between atoms.
rubric.description: A bond pair is a pair of electrons shared between two atoms to form a covalent bond.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a bond pair is shared between atoms.

rubric.why: A lone pair is defined by not participating in a bond.
rubric.description: A lone pair is a pair of valence electrons belonging to one atom and not shared in a bond.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a lone pair is unshared and belongs to one atom.

modelAnswer: A bond pair is a pair of electrons shared between two atoms to form a covalent bond.
A lone pair is a pair of valence electrons that is not shared in a bond.

items.followUp: State how many electrons atoms seek under the duet and octet rules.

rubric.why: Tests the stable electron arrangement described by the duet rule.
rubric.description: The duet rule states that an atom tends to achieve two electrons in its outermost shell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the duet rule involves two outer-shell electrons.

rubric.why: Tests the stable electron arrangement described by the octet rule.
rubric.description: The octet rule states that an atom tends to achieve eight electrons in its outermost shell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the octet rule involves eight outer-shell electrons.

modelAnswer: According to the duet rule, an atom tends to attain two electrons in its outermost shell.
According to the octet rule, an atom tends to attain eight electrons in its outermost shell.

rubric.why: A saturated solution contains as much dissolved solute as it can under the specified conditions.
rubric.description: It cannot dissolve any more solute at the stated temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that no more solute can dissolve.

rubric.description: The definition is understood at a specified temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for including the temperature condition.

modelAnswer: A saturated solution is one that cannot dissolve any more solute at a given temperature.

items.followUp: Define a solution and give an example of a solution in water.

rubric.why: An aqueous solution is specifically a solution with water as its solvent.
rubric.description: An aqueous solution is a solution in which water is the solvent.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying water as the solvent.

rubric.why: A suitable example demonstrates the meaning of aqueous solution.
rubric.description: A valid example is sodium chloride dissolved in water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example such as salt or sugar dissolved in water.

modelAnswer: An aqueous solution is a solution in which water is the solvent.
For example, sodium chloride dissolved in water forms an aqueous solution.

items.followUp: Define the concentration of a saturated solution in terms of solubility.

rubric.why: Solubility is measured as a specified amount of solute relative to solvent.
rubric.description: Solubility is the number of grams of solute that dissolve in 100 grams of solvent.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving the solute amount per 100 grams of solvent.

rubric.why: Solubility is defined for a saturated solution at a specified temperature.
rubric.description: The solution is saturated and the temperature is specified.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for including saturation and the temperature condition.

modelAnswer: Solubility is the number of grams of a solute that dissolve in 100 grams of solvent to form a saturated solution at a particular temperature.
